author: agent
text:
EDGE COLOUR IS BY KIND, INCLUDING WHEN LIT. Decided 2026-08-16, reversing an unrecorded choice from 8b3d174 (2026-08-10).

The template shipped with per-kind edge colours AND a `.link.lit{stroke:var(--amber)}` rule that overrode all of them. Both landed in the SAME commit, with no comment and no note, so eight days later nobody - including the author, who was me - could tell whether the flattening was a deliberate "one accent colour means selection" trade or an interaction nobody noticed. That ambiguity is the argument for this file's own product: the code could not say why, and the reason was not written down, so it stopped being knowable.

The reversal, and its cost, stated so the next person can weigh it rather than re-litigate it: selecting a node is the exact moment you want to know what reaches this and HOW, so the hue now carries kind and opacity/width carry the emphasis. The cost is that "which edges are selected" is no longer signalled by a single distinct colour - it reads as brightness against dimmed neighbours (resting opacity dropped .55 -> .28 to buy that contrast). If selection legibility ever loses against a busy graph, the fix is a stronger dim on non-selected edges, NOT a return to one colour for all kinds.

One variable per kind (--e-calls/--e-inherits/--e-imports/--e-contains) feeds three places that must agree: the legend swatch, the resting line, the lit line. Hard-coding a hex in any of them is how a legend comes to describe a colour the graph no longer draws. Kinds echo the node kind they concern - inherits takes the class colour, imports the module colour - and all four stay clear of --fresh (knowledge) and --beacon (stale) so an edge can never be misread as a verdict.
